lessonTitle: Germ Layer Derivatives and Neurulation: Neural Crest, Spina Bifida and Folic Acid

blocks.text: A melanocyte in your skin, a sympathetic neuron, the cells of your adrenal medulla and part of your jaw bone look nothing alike, yet they all descend from one transient group of cells that detach from the top of the folding neural tube in the fourth week. Where the three germ layers end up, and what happens when the neural tube fails to close, is the subject of this unit.

blocks.markdown: In week 3 gastrulation produces three **germ layers**: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. In weeks 3-8 these layers differentiate and fold, forming the basic organs. Knowing which layer gives rise to which tissue helps explain both normal anatomy and congenital disease.

rows: Epidermis, hair, nails, skin glands; lens of the eye; inner ear; enamel of teeth; anterior pituitary (from oral ectoderm); central nervous system (from neuroectoderm) including retina and posterior pituitary; and, via neural crest, peripheral nervous system and other structures

Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle; bone, cartilage and connective tissue; blood and blood vessels; heart; kidneys, gonads and genital ducts (intermediate mesoderm); spleen; adrenal cortex; serous membranes lining body cavities

Epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract and respiratory tract; liver and pancreas (parenchyma); epithelium of the bladder and urethra; thyroid and parathyroid glands; thymic epithelium; middle-ear and tonsil lining
blocks.caption: Principal derivatives of the three germ layers.

blocks.title: Assigning tissues to germ layers
blocks.prompt: State the germ layer of origin of (a) hepatocytes, (b) the cardiac muscle of the ventricle, (c) the epidermis, (d) the adrenal cortex and (e) the lens of the eye.

steps.text: (a) The liver develops as an outgrowth of the foregut epithelium, so hepatocytes are endoderm.
(b) The heart arises from splanchnic mesoderm, so cardiac muscle is mesoderm.
(c) The epidermis is formed from surface ectoderm.
(d) The adrenal cortex forms from mesoderm (while the medulla is derived from neural crest, which is an ectodermal derivative).
(e) The lens forms from a thickening of surface ectoderm (the lens placode), induced by the optic vesicle.

blocks.title: Neurulation
blocks.text: Neurulation is the process by which the neural plate folds and closes to form the neural tube, the primordium of the brain and spinal cord. It is induced by the notochord and occurs during weeks 3-4.

blocks.markdown: **Steps of neurulation.** (1) By about day 18 the notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken as the **neural plate**. (2) The plate's lateral edges rise as **neural folds**, with a central depression, the **neural groove**. (3) At the same time the neural folds move toward each other and fuse in the midline, beginning in the future **cervical region** around day 22. Fusion proceeds both cranially and caudally like a zip, converting the groove into the **neural tube**, which separates from the overlying surface ectoderm. (4) The unfused openings at each end are the **cranial (anterior) neuropore** and **caudal (posterior) neuropore**. The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal neuropore at about day 27-28, after which the lumen of the tube is sealed off from the amniotic cavity. The cranial end of the tube forms the brain vesicles and the rest forms the spinal cord.

**The neural crest.** As the neural folds fuse, cells at their crests (the border between neural tube and surface ectoderm) undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and **migrate** away as the **neural crest**. Because they become so many different tissues, the neural crest is sometimes called the 'fourth germ layer'. Derivatives include: sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia and enteric neurons; Schwann cells; **melanocytes**; **chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla**; much of the skeleton and connective tissue of the face and skull (craniofacial cartilage and bone); odontoblasts; and the aorticopulmonary septum of the heart. Failure of neural crest cells to colonise the distal bowel causes Hirschsprung disease (aganglionic megacolon).

blocks.title: Timeline of neural tube closure
blocks.prompt: An embryo is examined at day 24. Predict which part of the neural tube is closed and which parts are still open. Then state what would happen if the caudal neuropore failed to close.

steps.text: Fusion starts in the cervical region about day 22 and spreads both cranially and caudally, so by day 24 the middle portion is closed.
The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal neuropore at about day 27-28, so at day 24 both neuropores are still open and in communication with the amniotic cavity.
If the caudal neuropore fails to close, the lower part of the spinal cord and its coverings remain exposed or malformed, producing a lumbosacral neural tube defect (spina bifida).

blocks.answer: At day 24 the central portion is closed but both neuropores are open; failure of the caudal neuropore to close leads to a lumbosacral defect such as spina bifida.

blocks.markdown: **Neural tube defects (NTDs).** Failure of neural tube closure produces a group of defects. **Anencephaly** results from failure of the cranial neuropore to close; the forebrain and skull vault are largely absent, and it is incompatible with life. **Spina bifida** results from defective closure of the caudal neural tube and overlying vertebral arches, commonly in the lumbosacral region. Forms: **spina bifida occulta**, a vertebral arch defect covered by skin, often asymptomatic and sometimes marked by a tuft of hair or dimple; **meningocele**, a sac of meninges and CSF protruding through the defect, with the cord in place; and **myelomeningocele**, in which spinal cord tissue is also in the sac, causing lower-limb weakness, bladder and bowel dysfunction and often hydrocephalus. NTDs are multifactorial, with genetic and environmental contributions including maternal folate deficiency, diabetes and some anticonvulsants. Raised alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in maternal serum and amniotic fluid, together with the anomaly ultrasound, helps detect open NTDs.

rows: Absent forebrain and skull vault; incompatible with life; raised AFP; polyhydramnios
Fusion of the vertebral arch only
Often asymptomatic; skin-covered; may show hair tuft or dimple
Closure of caudal neural tube / vertebral arches
Meningeal sac with CSF; cord in normal position; usually mild neurological deficit
Cord and nerve roots in sac; leg weakness, bladder and bowel dysfunction, hydrocephalus
blocks.caption: Neural tube defects.

blocks.title: Folic acid and neural tube defects
blocks.text: Peri-conceptional folic acid (a B vitamin needed for nucleotide synthesis and methylation) reduces the occurrence and recurrence of NTDs. Supplementation must start before conception and continue through the first trimester, because the neural tube closes by about day 28, often before pregnancy is recognised. Guidelines commonly advise 400 micrograms daily for women planning pregnancy and a higher dose for women with a previous NTD-affected pregnancy; exact doses vary by guideline (this is a teaching example and not personal medical advice). Food fortification programmes have also lowered NTD rates.

blocks.title: Expected number of cases and effect of folic acid
blocks.prompt: In a population the NTD rate is 1.5 per 1000 pregnancies. Folic acid supplementation (illustratively) lowers the rate by 60%. How many NTD-affected pregnancies are expected among 20,000 pregnancies without supplementation, and with universal supplementation?
blocks.answer: 30 cases without supplementation and 12 with it, so 18 are prevented in 20,000 pregnancies.

items: Ectoderm: epidermis, CNS, lens; mesoderm: muscle, bone, blood, kidney; endoderm: gut and airway lining, liver, pancreas.
Neurulation: notochord induces the neural plate, folds fuse from the cervical region, neuropores close at about days 25 and 27-28.
Neural crest: dorsal root ganglia, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, facial skeleton.
Spina bifida and anencephaly result from failure of neural tube closure; folic acid reduces risk.

blocks.title: Neural crest versus neural tube
blocks.text: Neural tube gives the CNS and the retina and the neurons and glia within it. Neural crest gives the PNS and many non-neural tissues. Do not confuse the two.

points: Ectoderm forms the epidermis and nervous system, mesoderm forms muscle, bone, blood and kidneys, and endoderm forms the lining of the gut and airway with their glands.
Neurulation turns the neural plate into the neural tube; neural crest cells migrate from the folds to form many structures including the peripheral nervous system and melanocytes.
Failure of neural tube closure causes anencephaly or spina bifida; peri-conceptional folic acid reduces the risk.

questions.stem: Which tissue is derived from endoderm?

options.text: Epithelial lining of the small intestine

questions.correctOptionText: Epithelial lining of the small intestine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the epithelium of the gut tube is endodermal.
distractorRationale.d: The kidney's nephron is derived from intermediate mesoderm.

questions.explanation: The gut tube is formed from endoderm, so its epithelial lining is endodermal; the muscle and connective tissue in its wall come from mesoderm.

questions.stem: Which structure is derived from neural crest?

options.text: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla

questions.correctOptionText: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the adrenal medulla derives from neural crest.
distractorRationale.b: The adrenal cortex is derived from mesoderm.
distractorRationale.c: Spinal cord neurons come from the neural tube itself.

questions.explanation: Neural crest cells migrate to form the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, whereas the cortex is mesodermal. Spinal cord neurons come from the neural tube.

questions.stem: A newborn has a skin-covered, fluctuant lumbar sac that contains CSF and meninges. The spinal cord is in its normal position and neurological examination is normal. What is the diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: meninges and CSF herniate but the cord is not in the sac.
distractorRationale.b: In myelomeningocele neural tissue lies in the sac and deficits are present.
distractorRationale.c: Anencephaly is a cranial defect, not a lumbar sac.
distractorRationale.d: Spina bifida occulta has no sac; only a vertebral arch defect.

questions.explanation: A sac of meninges and CSF with the cord in place defines a meningocele. If neural tissue were in the sac it would be a myelomeningocele, with neurological deficit.

questions.stem: Why must folic acid supplementation begin before conception to reduce the risk of neural tube defects?

options.text: The neural tube closes by about the fourth week, often before the pregnancy is recognised
Folic acid is not absorbed during pregnancy
The neural tube closes in the third trimester
Folic acid acts only on the placenta

questions.correctOptionText: The neural tube closes by about the fourth week, often before the pregnancy is recognised

distractorRationale.a: Correct: closure completes at about day 28, so supplements must be present early.
distractorRationale.b: Folic acid is absorbed during pregnancy; timing is the issue.
distractorRationale.c: Neural tube closure occurs in week 4, not the third trimester.
distractorRationale.d: Its protective effect concerns neural tube closure, not the placenta.

questions.explanation: Closure of the caudal neuropore occurs by about day 28 after fertilisation, which is early in pregnancy and often before a missed period. Folate stores must therefore be adequate before conception to protect closure.

questions.stem: Failure of the cranial neuropore to close is associated with which finding?

options.text: Anencephaly with raised maternal serum AFP
Spina bifida occulta with normal AFP
Isolated cleft of the vertebral body

questions.correctOptionText: Anencephaly with raised maternal serum AFP

distractorRationale.a: Correct: open cranial defect gives anencephaly, and AFP leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal serum.
distractorRationale.b: Spina bifida occulta concerns the caudal vertebral arches and is closed by skin.
distractorRationale.c: Hirschsprung disease is due to failed neural crest migration into the bowel.
distractorRationale.d: A vertebral body cleft is a different malformation.

questions.explanation: The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25; failure of closure results in anencephaly. Because the defect is open, fetal AFP leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal serum, raising levels.

questions.stem: In a region the rate of neural tube defects is 2 per 1000 pregnancies. A fortification programme is estimated (illustratively) to reduce the rate by 65%. How many NTD-affected pregnancies are expected per 50,000 pregnancies after fortification? Give your answer as a number of pregnancies.
questions.explanation: Baseline cases = 50,000 x 2/1000 = 100. A 65% reduction leaves 35% of cases: 100 x 0.35 = 35. Folate fortification and supplementation reduce NTDs but do not abolish them since they are multifactorial.

questions.stem: True or false: Melanocytes of the skin are derived from the neural crest.
questions.explanation: Neural crest cells migrate to the skin and differentiate into melanocytes. This is why neural crest defects can cause pigmentation anomalies.

questions.stem: List the major tissues derived from each of the three germ layers, giving at least three examples per layer.
markingGuide: Ectoderm: epidermis, hair and nails, lens, inner ear, nervous system (CNS and, via neural crest, PNS), enamel, anterior pituitary.
Mesoderm: skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle, bone, cartilage, connective tissue, blood and vessels, heart, kidney and gonads, spleen, adrenal cortex.
Endoderm: epithelial lining of the GI and respiratory tracts, liver, pancreas, thyroid, parathyroids, thymic epithelium, bladder lining.
At least three correct examples for each layer.
questions.explanation: Each layer gives specific tissues: ectoderm gives surface and nervous tissue, mesoderm gives supportive and circulatory tissues, endoderm gives epithelial linings and glands of the gut and airway.

questions.stem: Describe the process of neurulation and the origin of the neural crest, and give four derivatives of the neural crest.
markingGuide: Notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate.
Neural plate folds to form neural folds and groove; folds fuse beginning in the cervical region, forming the neural tube.
Neuropores close: cranial at about day 25, caudal at about day 27-28.
Neural crest cells arise from the crests of the neural folds and migrate after epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
Derivatives: dorsal root ganglia, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, craniofacial skeleton, autonomic ganglia (any four).
questions.explanation: The neural tube forms by plate folding and fusion; the crest cells that leave the folds give rise to diverse derivatives including peripheral nerves and melanocytes.

questions.stem: Explain how failed neural tube closure produces spina bifida and anencephaly, distinguish meningocele from myelomeningocele, and explain how folic acid reduces risk.
markingGuide: Anencephaly: failure of the cranial neuropore to close (about day 25), leaving forebrain and skull vault undeveloped.
Spina bifida: failure of caudal neural tube and vertebral arch closure; caudal neuropore (about day 27-28).

Meningocele: sac of meninges and CSF, cord normally positioned, usually little deficit; myelomeningocele: spinal cord and nerve roots in sac with leg weakness, bladder and bowel problems and hydrocephalus.
Folic acid supplementation before conception and in early pregnancy reduces incidence and recurrence of NTDs; closure occurs by week 4.
NTDs are multifactorial; AFP is raised.
questions.explanation: NTDs reflect failure of fusion of the neural folds. The differences between meningocele and myelomeningocele relate to whether neural tissue is herniated. Folate supports closure early in development.
